text:
The NMES1988 data describe 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. It details several variables with the outcome variable being number of physician office visits. The rest are listed below

The visits outcome is a count. Whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed. The variance (45.69) is about 7.91 times the mean (5.77). 16% of people had no visits. The greatest number of visits reported (89)is a shockingly large number, but could be legitimate.









A linear model is a poor choice for the visits outcome variable because the visits data are counts, meaning that negative visits and half visits are impossible/meaningless values. This is evidenced by the DHARMa simulations. The residuals, shown in the QQ plot, do not follow the expected flat diagonal line. The outlier and KS tests also speak to this concern. In the residual-vs-predicted plot, as the predicted probability approaches 1, the distribution becomes more compressed toward the lower end of residual values. This is also evidenced by the red 0.5 quantile line. Taken together, its clear these data are not a good fit for a Gaussian model.

For the comparison between M0 and M1, nested χ² = 2,175.428, p <.001. For the comparison between M1 and M2, nested χ² = 959.924, p <.001. Both of these likelihood-ratio tests indicate a statistically significant improvement in model fit. This means that adding the additional predictors improved the model fit across both comparisons, suggesting that M2 is a better fit model than M1 and M0. Further, the AIC and BIC decreased for both comparisons, once again implying that M2 is a good model to select. For these reasons, I have selected M2 as the ideal model.
The provisionally selected model is M2: Full.
